title: How much hydrogen awaits us underground?
gist: Geologic (naturally occurring underground) hydrogen has attracted dozens of startups including Bill Gates-backed Koloma and Australia's HyTerra, but despite USGS estimates of trillions of tons in Earth's crust, no commercially viable reservoir has yet been reported and companies are withholding data while raising money. The measured flows now being documented are small — roughly 140 metric tons per year escaping Canada's Kidd Creek mine and at least 200 t/yr from Albania's Bulqizë chromium mine — pushing the field toward a second path: ARPA-E-funded stimulated production aiming for a 10,000x reaction-rate acceleration, with an Oman water-injection well recently producing 90% hydrogen gas.

themes.theme: Resource-size hype versus zero proven commercial reservoirs

insights.claim: The US Geological Survey estimates trillions of tons of H2 are produced within Earth's crust, and recovering even a small fraction would meet global hydrogen demand for centuries — the headline number driving the entire geologic hydrogen exploration boom.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: The resource-in-place figure is enormous but says nothing about recoverability — the classic resource-versus-reserve distinction that has burned commodity investors before.
insights.locator: Researchers at the US Geological Survey have estimated

insights.claim: No one has yet reported finding a commercially viable reservoir of geologic hydrogen despite a worldwide exploration effort involving dozens of startups, meaning the sector is still pre-discovery after years of capital deployment.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: The core investment case remains unproven — treat geologic hydrogen equity as venture-stage exploration risk, not as an energy-supply story.
insights.quote: No one has yet reported finding a commercially viable reservoir of the gas
insights.locator: But the search so far has come up short

insights.claim: Public data on geologic hydrogen discoveries is deliberately scarce because companies are jockeying for position and seeking to attract investment, creating an information asymmetry between operators and outside capital.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: Opaque disclosure in a pre-revenue exploration sector is a classic setup for valuation inflation; academic publications like the Kidd Creek study are currently the only independent read.
insights.quote: public data on what has been found remains in short supply as companies jockey for position and seek to attract investment
insights.locator: But the search so far has come up short

insights.claim: Grenoble geochemist Laurent Truche frames the field's remaining hurdle as purely economic rather than scientific — natural hydrogen's existence is settled, but economic and reliable production at commercial scale is not.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: A useful diligence filter: dismiss pitches that argue existence and demand evidence on flow rates, well economics and reliability instead.
insights.quote: The remaining challenge is not proving that natural hydrogen exists, but proving that it can be produced economically and reliably at commercial scale

themes.theme: Measured flow rates set the realistic ceiling

insights.claim: Analysis of 35 boreholes tracked over more than a decade at Ontario's Kidd Creek mine found each borehole consistently released an average of eight kilograms of hydrogen per year, implying roughly 140 metric tons per year escaping unused from the mine's more than 14,000 boreholes.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: A concrete, peer-reviewed per-borehole yield benchmark against which any startup's claimed flow rates can be sanity-checked.
insights.locator: At Kidd Creek mine, Sherwood Lollar and her colleague Oliver Warr

insights.claim: The Kidd Creek total of roughly 140 metric tons per year is explicitly characterized as not a world-changing amount, and its realistic best use would be powering a substantial portion of the mine's own operations rather than supplying an external market.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: The near-term commercial shape of geologic hydrogen is behind-the-meter, site-captive supply for the host operation — not merchant hydrogen volumes.
insights.quote: This tally, published earlier this year in the journal PNAS, is not a world-changing amount
insights.locator: This tally, published earlier this year

insights.claim: Truche's team reported in 2024 that at least 200 metric tons of hydrogen flow annually out of the Bulqizë chromium mine in Albania, making mine ventilation shafts the most concretely documented sources of natural hydrogen flux to date.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: Existing metal mines are the cheapest place to prove the concept — watch mining operators, not dedicated hydrogen explorers, for the first real production.

insights.claim: Geologic hydrogen is generated by two distinct mechanisms — water molecules split by chemical reactions with iron-rich rock, or split by the radioactive decay of other elements as at Kidd Creek — which means prospective geology is not a single play type.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: Two generation mechanisms imply two separate exploration models; a company's geological thesis determines whether its acreage is even the right rock type.
insights.locator: A flurry of exploration efforts have launched

themes.theme: Stimulated production as the alternative path to scale

insights.claim: Rather than hunting for reservoirs, researchers and startups are pursuing stimulated hydrogen — injecting water, heat or catalysts into reactive rocks to force the gas-producing reaction — reframing the opportunity from exploration to engineered manufacturing.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: Stimulation converts a discovery lottery into a repeatable engineering problem, which is a far more investable structure if the reaction rates can be hit.
insights.quote: Proof, however, doesn’t necessarily require striking the mother lode.

insights.claim: ARPA-E funds more than a dozen stimulated-hydrogen projects and has set an explicit target of accelerating the hydrogen-producing reaction by a factor of 10,000, the rate researchers estimate is needed for commercial viability.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: A published 10,000x threshold gives a hard, checkable milestone — any stimulated-hydrogen claim can be benchmarked against it before capital is committed.
insights.locator: More than a dozen of these projects are funded by ARPA-E

insights.claim: In Oman, a team drilled a one-kilometer borehole, injected 50,000 cubic meters of water into the rock, and on reopening the well several months later found gas spewing out at 90% hydrogen — the most striking field indication so far that stimulation may work.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: A 90%-purity result from a single injection well is the sector's most important recent datapoint; confirmation would sharply re-rate stimulated-hydrogen ventures.
insights.locator: An indication that this could work came earlier this year

insights.claim: The Oman result is not yet interpretable because the crucial question is unresolved: whether the hydrogen coming out of the well was manufactured by the water injection or had simply been there all along.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: Attribution risk means the headline Oman number should not yet be underwritten — wait for isotopic or mass-balance confirmation before treating stimulation as proven.
insights.quote: Is the hydrogen rising up out of the well made through stimulation, or had it been there all along?
insights.locator: The most crucial question is a basic one

themes.theme: Why underground hydrogen changes the economics at all

insights.claim: Conventional hydrogen production typically generates large greenhouse-gas emissions and consumes more energy than the resulting gas contains, which is precisely why ready-made underground reservoirs would change the economics of hydrogen as a fuel.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: Geologic hydrogen's entire value proposition is bypassing the negative energy balance of electrolytic and steam-reformed hydrogen — the threat vector for incumbent green-hydrogen project economics.
insights.quote: producing it typically generates lots of greenhouse-gas emissions and requires more energy than the gas contains
insights.locator: While hydrogen fuel does show promise

insights.claim: Australian firm HyTerra and Bill Gates-backed Koloma have both been exploring the US Midwest to reach ancient oceanic rocks associated with hydrogen production, concentrating early private capital on a specific North American geological play.
insights.speaker: James Dinneen
insights.so_what: HyTerra is a listed vehicle and Koloma a marquee Gates-backed private name — the two most direct ways to track sentiment in the geologic hydrogen trade.
insights.locator: The hunt has spread all over the world
